Simulation: do the oversight metrics work?¶

What this notebook does. It creates simulated caseworkers with different behaviours (attentive, "sees but doesn't act", rubber-stamper, distrustful, fatigued), has them review the households of the S8 sample, and checks whether our metrics can tell them apart. It then simulates a year of production to see whether and when the monitor notices a decline in oversight, and computes how many caseworkers and cases the audit needs.

What it does NOT do. It does not say how real caseworkers behave. We set the behaviours ourselves with parameters. The simulation is a way to test the measuring instruments: if a metric cannot separate caseworkers built on purpose to be different, it will not work on real ones.

Structure

  1. The simulated world: households, reference, data errors, suggestion with errors
  2. The caseworker model
  3. The metrics (from Passi & Vorvoreanu and from the brief)
  4. Experiment 1 – which metrics separate which behaviours
  5. Experiment 2 – the monitor in production: does it notice the decline? How fast? With how many false alarms?
  6. Experiment 3 – audit power: how many caseworkers and cases to detect a 15-point drop
  7. Validation: recomputing the official table
  8. What we learned, and limitations

The functions are in simcore.py (simulation) and didattica_en.py (explanatory figures), next to this notebook.

1. The simulated world¶

We start from the 1,900 households in S8 and build four things.

1a. The reference ("right answer"). In S8 the outcome follows no rule (we saw this in the data analysis), so we cannot use it. Instead we apply the rule described in the UNHCR guidance to the true scores: negative administrative checks → excluded; score below the targeting threshold (24.4, an assumption) → excluded; then the monthly ranking: the first k are included, the next w go on the waiting list, the rest are excluded. k and w for each month are the real S8 counts. Coding: 0 = excluded, 1 = waiting list, 2 = included.

1b. Errors in the recorded data. In 10% of households one factor is recorded one level off (like case F-0733 in the prototype). The calculation on the recorded data can therefore be wrong.

1c. The AI suggestion. It is the calculation on the recorded data, plus 18% model errors (the suggestion is moved to another outcome), to approach Cashy's error rate on eligibility.

1d. How recognisable each error is. Not every error can be seen from the case file.

  • Recognisable (1.0): the error comes from wrong data (the interviewer disagrees), or the household is far from the cut-off (more than 5 points), so the right outcome is obvious.
  • Hard to recognise (0.3): the household is close to the cut-off and the error is a "budget" error: almost impossible to see by looking at the file.

2. The caseworker model¶

For each case, every simulated caseworker follows the steps of our review:

1. INDEPENDENT DECISION   right with probability  skill      (otherwise one of the other two outcomes)
2. SEES THE SUGGESTION    if the AI is wrong, notices it with probability  d × recognisability
                          if the AI is right, still believes it is wrong with probability  fa  (false alarm)
3. GIVES A 1–5 RATING     1–2 if they think the suggestion is wrong, 3–5 otherwise
4. FINAL DECISION         • if they think the AI is wrong: follows it anyway with probability  c_lo  ("sees but doesn't act"),
                            otherwise keeps their own decision (or corrects it, if it matched the AI)
                          • if they think the AI is right and their decision was different: switches to the AI with probability  c_hi
                            (sometimes only halfway, e.g. from "excluded" to "waiting list")

The parameters define the profiles:

In [4]:

skill (right initial decision) d (notices the error) fa (false alarm) c_hi (follows the AI when they think it is right) c_lo (follows the AI even when they think it is wrong)
Attentive 0.80 0.85 0.05 0.85 0.05
Sees but doesn't act 0.80 0.85 0.05 0.90 0.55
Rubber-stamper 0.65 0.30 0.03 0.95 0.70
Distrustful 0.75 0.60 0.35 0.15 0.02
  • Attentive: notices errors and does not follow the AI when they think it is wrong.
  • Sees but doesn't act: notices errors like the attentive caseworker, but follows the AI anyway in 55% of cases. This is the behaviour that emerged in the experiment with the "Responsible AI" statements.
  • Rubber-stamper: notices little and almost always follows the AI.
  • Distrustful: overrides the AI on principle, even when it is right (overriding "to make the numbers").
  • Fatigued (not in the table): starts like the attentive caseworker and, over the session, notices fewer errors and follows the AI more.

3. The metrics¶

Metric Definition Needs the right answer? Source
Switch fraction Among cases where the independent decision differed from the AI, share where the final decision switched to the AI No Lu & Yin 2021, in Passi & Vorvoreanu
Mean WOA Weight of Advice: (final − initial) / (AI − initial), on the three ordered outcomes. 0 = ignores the AI, 1 = adopts it No Logg et al. 2019
Judgment–action inconsistency Among cases rated 1–2, share where the suggestion is accepted anyway No Result of the Cashy experiment
Initial agreement with the AI Share of cases where the independent decision already matches the AI No Lu & Yin 2021
Correct override / Over-reliance On cases where the AI is wrong: share where the final decision differs from / equals the suggestion Yes Brief, Buçinca 2021
Under-reliance On cases where the AI is right: share where the final decision differs from the suggestion Yes Brief
WOA split by correctness WOA when the AI is wrong and when it is right; the difference measures how well the caseworker discriminates Yes Our extension of WOA
Shared error Cases with a wrong AI where the independent decision was also wrong in the same way Yes "Human errors", Buçinca 2021

The metrics that do not need the right answer can be computed on every production case. Those that need it can only be computed on sentinel cases or in the audit.

4. Experiment 1 – which metrics separate which behaviours¶

Each profile reviews 2,000 cases drawn from S8. With this many cases the metrics are stable, so the differences depend only on behaviour, not on chance.

How to read the table¶

Metrics that can be gamed:

  • Correct override on its own. The Distrustful profile has the highest value of all (0.88), higher than the attentive one, but only because it overrides everything: its under-reliance is 0.48 and its final accuracy is the worst (0.56). This is why the brief asks to always report the four measures together: a single one rewards those who override "to make the numbers".
  • Switch fraction and mean WOA on their own. They rank the profiles well on the "how much do they follow the AI" axis (Distrustful 0.07 → Rubber-stamper 0.85), but they don't say whether following it was right. A middle value, like the attentive one (0.47), can hide both good and bad behaviour. Their value lies in change over time, not in the level (see Experiment 2).

Metrics that really discriminate:

  • WOA discrimination (WOA when the AI is right minus WOA when it is wrong): attentive is at 0.51, all others below 0.22. It is the only metric that separates the attentive profile from all the others, but it needs the reference.
  • Judgment–action inconsistency: without a reference, it clearly separates "sees but doesn't act" (0.56) and "rubber-stamper" (0.71) from attentive (0.06). It is the most useful metric to compute on every case.
  • Fatigued: over a whole session its values sit between attentive and "sees but doesn't act". It shows up better when the metric is tracked along the session, as in the chart below.

The same information as a picture: each profile is a point. Horizontal: how much it follows the AI when the AI is right. Vertical: how much it follows it when the AI is wrong. A good caseworker sits bottom right, far from the diagonal.

Computing the metrics by position in the session makes fatigue visible (Ray et al. 2026: a sustained decline from the baseline). In practice this means comparing the first cases of the day with the last ones, always in aggregate form.

5. Experiment 2 – the monitor in production¶

Scenario: 3 offices (A, B, C), 8 caseworkers each, 12 months. Each caseworker reviews 40 cases a month, plus 2 sentinel cases (one where the AI is wrong in a recognisable way, one where the AI is right). For the first 6 months everyone is "attentive". From month 7, in one office, the caseworkers change behaviour.

The monitor computes every month, per office:

  • switch fraction and judgment–action inconsistency on all cases (no reference needed, 320 cases a month);
  • correct override and under-reliance on the sentinel cases only (reference needed, 8 cases a month of each type).

The alarm rule is a control chart: the mean of months 1–6 is the baseline; an alarm fires if a month moves more than 3 standard errors in the "bad" direction. This is the operational definition of Ray et al. (2026).

The two metrics without a reference, computed on hundreds of cases, jump immediately in month 7. Correct override on the sentinels also drops, but it is much noisier, because each month rests on only 8 cases.

Now we repeat the year 300 times for each scenario and count how often, and when, the alarm fires.

How the alarm rule works, for a single metric and a single office:

def run_scenario(drift,reps=300,seed=0):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed); R=[alarms(monitor_run(W,rng,drift=drift)) for _ in range(reps)]
    keys=R[0].keys(); P=pd.Series({k:np.mean([not np.isnan(r[k]) for r in R]) for k in keys})
    Md=pd.Series({k:(np.nanmedian([r[k] for r in R]) if any(not np.isnan(r[k]) for r in R) else np.nan) for k in keys})
    return P,Md
NOMI={'sw':'Switch fraction ↑','sw_down':'Switch fraction ↓','ga':'Judgment–action ↑','co':'Correct override ↓ (sent.)','ur':'Under-reliance ↑ (sent.)'}
SCEN={"Sees but doesn't act (office B)":{'B':'Vede ma non agisce'},'Slight decline (office B)':{'B':'Calo lieve'},
      'Overrides to make the numbers (office C)':{'C':'Diffidente'},'No change':{}}
tab={}
for nome,dr in SCEN.items():
    P,Md=run_scenario(dr)
    uff=list(dr)[0] if dr else 'A'
    for k in NOMI:
        tab[(nome,NOMI[k])]=dict(**{'P(alarm) changed office' if dr else 'P(false alarm) office A':P[(uff,k)],
                                 'median month':Md[(uff,k)]},
                                 **({'P(false alarm) other offices':np.mean([P[(o,k)] for o in 'ABC' if o!=uff])} if dr else {}))
T=pd.DataFrame(tab).T; T.round(2)

How to read the results¶

  • "Sees but doesn't act": switch fraction and judgment–action fire in 100% of the simulations, already in month 7, i.e. immediately. Correct override on the sentinels almost always catches it, but often a month later.
  • Slight decline (caseworkers follow the wrong AI in 20% of cases instead of 5%): only judgment–action always catches it, and immediately. Switch fraction catches it about 7 times in 10, the sentinels about 1 in 2. They are too few cases a month for a small decline.
  • "Overrides to make the numbers": the most instructive case. Correct override gives no alarm at all; it actually improves. A monitor based only on overrides would read it as a success. It is caught instead by the falling switch fraction and by under-reliance on the concordant sentinels. This is why the sentinels must include cases where the AI is right, and why the monitor must look in both directions.
  • False alarms: about 2–8% per metric and per office over 6 months. The sentinel metrics give more (about 10%), because with few cases the control-chart approximation is less precise. This is why an alarm triggers an event to be explained, not a sanction.

Conclusion: the metrics without a reference are fast and sensitive; the sentinels are slow but necessary to know whether the change is good or bad, and to catch those who override to make the numbers. Both are needed.

6. Experiment 3 – audit power¶

The brief's question: what is the smallest audit (caseworkers and cases) that detects a 15-point drop in correct override with 80% power?

The model. Two groups of caseworkers (e.g. current screen vs new review). In group 1 mean correct override is 90%, in group 2 it is 75%. Each caseworker has their own tendency (a random effect on the logit with standard deviation σ): ratings from the same caseworker are not independent, as the brief requires. Each caseworker reviews m discordant cases. The test compares per-caseworker proportions (the caseworker is the unit of analysis), with a two-sided Welch t-test at 5%. We repeat each combination 2,000 times and count how often the test detects the difference.

σ = 0.9 corresponds to an intra-caseworker correlation (ICC) of about 0.2. We vary it to see how much it matters.

Why the caseworker is the unit of analysis. Ratings from the same caseworker resemble each other: if a caseworker tends to follow the AI, they do it on all their cases. Counting 200 ratings as if they were 200 different people overstates what we know. Here is a simulated audit with 20 caseworkers per group:

Design of the original experiment (13 vs 18 caseworkers, 2 discordant cases each, σ = 0.9):
  power for an effect as large as the observed one (96% → 67%): 0.83
  power for a 15-point drop (90% → 75%):                         0.30

   2 cases per caseworker → at least >60 caseworkers per group needed
   4 cases per caseworker → at least 40 caseworkers per group needed
   6 cases per caseworker → at least 30 caseworkers per group needed
   8 cases per caseworker → at least 25 caseworkers per group needed
  12 cases per caseworker → at least 25 caseworkers per group needed

How to read the results¶

  • The original design (13 vs 18 caseworkers, 2 discordant cases each) had power 0.83 for the large effect it found, but only 0.30 for a 15-point drop. An audit with that design would miss 7 out of 10 drops of that size.
  • More cases per caseworker help a lot, but only up to a point. Going from 2 to 8 cases greatly reduces the number of caseworkers needed. Beyond that the gain shrinks, because the difference between caseworkers (σ) does not shrink when each one reviews more cases.
  • With σ = 0.9 you need about 25 caseworkers per group with 8 discordant cases each, about 40 with 4 cases, about 60 (borderline) with 2 cases. If caseworkers differ a lot from each other (σ = 1.4) you need about 40–50 caseworkers per group even with many cases. σ should be estimated from the S4 data, if we get access to it.
  • Consequence for the design: more discordant cases per caseworker, balanced between wrong inclusions and wrong exclusions and across different cases, instead of 2 fixed cases. This also solves the problem of case and error direction being confounded.

7. Validation: recomputing the official table¶

The audit kit must reproduce the numbers in the brief. Without S4 we can at least recompute the Wilson intervals from the counts.

     ('Plain AI','Final accuracy'):(54,65),('Statements','Correct override'):(24,36),('Statements','Over-reliance'):(12,36),
     ('Statements','Correct acceptance'):(36,36),('Statements','Final accuracy'):(62,90)}
rows=[]
for (g,mtr),(k,n) in uff.items():
    lo,hi=proportion_confint(k,n,method='wilson'); rows.append([g,mtr,f"{k}/{n}",f"{100*k/n:.1f}%",f"[{100*lo:.1f}, {100*hi:.1f}]"])
pd.DataFrame(rows,columns=['Group','Measure','Count','%','95% Wilson CI'])

The intervals match those in the brief (e.g. 96.2% [81.1, 99.3] and 66.7% [50.3, 79.8]). With S4 we could also verify the calculation from the individual reviews.

8. What we learned¶

# Result Consequence for the project
1 Correct override on its own rewards those who override everything Always report the four measures; the sentinels must also include cases where the AI is right
2 Switch fraction and WOA measure how much the AI is followed, not whether it should be Use them for change over time, not as a level
3 WOA discrimination is the only measure that separates the attentive profile from all others Compute it in the audit and on the sentinels
4 Judgment–action inconsistency detects "sees but doesn't act" without knowing the right answer Main metric of the daily monitor
5 Metrics without a reference detect a decline in the same month; the sentinels are slower Two-level monitor: daily metrics + verification sentinels
6 "Overriding to make the numbers" improves correct override The monitor looks in both directions (falling switch fraction, under-reliance on sentinels)
7 The original design has power 0.30 for a 15-point drop Audit with about 8 discordant cases per caseworker and about 25 caseworkers per group (with σ = 0.9)
8 Fatigue shows up when comparing the start and end of a session Metrics by position in the session, in aggregate form

Limitations¶

  • The behaviours are invented. The profile parameters are plausible assumptions, not estimates. The simulation shows that the metrics can separate those behaviours, not that real caseworkers behave that way.
  • The reference is constructed with the rule from the UNHCR guidance and an assumed targeting threshold, because in S8 the outcome follows no rule.
  • Error recognisability (1.0 or 0.3) is a simplification.
  • The 1–5 rating is linked to error perception in a simple way; in reality it is noisier.
  • σ (difference between caseworkers) must be estimated from real data: it changes the number of caseworkers needed a lot.
  • False alarms of the sentinel metrics are somewhat high because the normal approximation is imprecise with few cases; with real data an exact test or pooling two months is preferable.

All results are properties of the simulation on S8, not of the UNHCR operation.
